newsitem.title: UK: Minor metals - Molybdenum features, rhodium dives.
newsitem.headline: Minor metals - Molybdenum features, rhodium dives.

text.p: Molybdenum held the spotlight in minor metals trading this week, though conditions remained slow throughout the sector amid the lack of strong consumer demand, traders said.
Elsewhere, rhodium dived under U.S. speculative selling, while recent star performer cobalt, slipped slightly as upside sentiment took a knock from trader profit-taking.
Merchant buying and consumer short-covering against the backdrop of tight nearby supplies chased molybdenum higher, though volumes remained light.
Traders said the market was further bolstered by a shortage of concentrate and a lack of Chinese offers.
"The Chinese have backed off, they are not selling at the moment," one London trader said.
Traders noted news that lower metal grades at Codelco's Chuquicamata mine in Chile would cause molybdenum output to drop to around 30 million pounds this year from 37 million in 1995.
Traders opinions remained divided as to whether the market can sustain its spike higher.
"Even the producers are short which is likely to see further short-covering," one commented.
But another said "there is a bottleneck at present, though this is likely to evaporate between Novemeber and December."
All agreed nearby stocks were accounted for by long term contracts between producers and consumers.
Rhodium prices, reeling from U.S. speculator selling over the last week, moved towards $200 an ounce, where prices were expected to level off.

Rhodium is now around $245, close to a January 1996 low and the mid-1980s nadir of around $230 -- a major retracement from dizzy heights of $7,000 reached in 1990 as booming demand from autocatalyst makers burnt off global supplies.
Traders said estimates of the recent selling varied considerably, from as much as 1.25 tonnes (72,000 ounces) down to a more conservative 5,000 ounces.
"I believe the bottom of the market is towards $200 where buying is expected to come into play," a trader said.
The recent uptick in cobalt slowed in quiet conditions.

Traders failed to agree on the next price direction for cobalt. Several suggested the lack of upside progress, after Russian material recovered from the recent 23-month low of around $18/$19 per pound was a signal that the market had little to do on the upside.
"I am taking another look at the fundamentals," one trader said adding he was tempted to sell at current levels.
He said production was set to rise over the coming years which could balance supply and demand.
Others were quick to dispute this scenario, believing many of the planned production hikes were unlikely to come on stream.
They also suggested the market was still running tight amid the lack of readily available Zambian and Russian material.
Other traders suggested the lack of upside progress in Russian cobalt stemmed from a major North American producer faling to lift their prices.
"They (the producer) are still selling at levels below true market value...a situation that is hampering upside moves," a trader said.
News last week that major producer China was to cut production of antimony by 20 percent in the next few months held few surprises to Europen traders.
Prices failed to move significantly on the announcement and drifted slightly lower.
Traders said they were unsure that Chinese officials could enforce the planned cuts. "Its been tried before and failed," one trader said.
He explained that compared to the north, the south of China was more Westernised with many of the antimony facilities leased from the Chinese government by private enterprise.
Manganese climbed higher amid the lack of prompt material, while the other minor metals in slack business held little changed levels.
